system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 8 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2187-01-30 18:28:00 to 2187-02-07 15:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with cholangiocarcinoma and a history of recurrent cholangitis, was admitted with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and low-grade fever. Imaging revealed an enlarging liver abscess, and he was started on meropenem. Due to prior ERCP-related bleeding, biliary intervention was avoided. Percutaneous abscess drainage yielded multidrug-resistant E. coli, resistant to his home suppressive antibiotics. He was transitioned to ceftazidime/avibactam and metronidazole. A new portal vein thrombus was identified and treated with anticoagulation using apixaban. Ursodiol was initiated to address biliary sludge. His infection resolved, and he was discharged with a PICC line for continued IV antibiotics, outpatient follow-up, and a plan for 4–6 weeks of antimicrobial therapy.
problems: Unspecified Escherichia coli [E. coli] as the cause of diseases classified elsewhere
Benign prostatic hyperplasia without lower urinary tract symptoms

onapixaban with ERCP ___ c/b portobiliary fistula and active bleeding
requiring ___ stent x 2 to R posterior portal vein,recent completion of 4 weeks
of IV ceftaz-avibactum for MDR ecoli hepatic abscess with oral flagyl,
presents today with 1 day of fever, nausea, malaise.// f/u liver abscess

TECHNIQUE:  T1- and T2-weighted multiplanar images of the abdomen were
acquired in a 1.5 T magnet.
Intravenous contrast: 9 mL Gadavist.

COMPARISON:  Prior MRCP dated ___.

FINDINGS: 

Lower Thorax: There is trace pleural fluid bilaterally without frank effusion.
There is bibasilar dependent atelectasis.  There is no pericardial effusion.

Liver: Diffuse left hepatic atrophy is re-demonstrated, similar to the recent
prior study.  There are unchanged geographic areas of arterial
hyperenhancement suggesting underlying cholangitis.  New T2 hyperintense, T1
hypointense nonenhancing hepatic collections with surrounding hyperemia within
segment VIII are consistent with microabscesses with the largest microabscess
measuring up to 0.8 x 0.7 cm (1401:70).  Additional smaller microabscesses are
present as well (1401:66, 41, 35).  There is no drainable collection. There is
no definite focal lesion.  An area of wedge-shaped enhancement with washout
and associated capsular retraction in segment VI is unchanged from prior
studies and may represent fibrosis following prior portal venous thrombus
(1401:93, 1402:93).

Biliary: Mild right-sided intrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation is similar to
the prior study.  There is diffuse irregular biliary ductal dilatation within
the atrophic left lobe.  Stents within the common bile duct are noted in
unchanged location.

Pancreas: There is loss of the normal T1 hyperintensity within the pancreatic
head and uncinate process with relative preservation of portions of the
pancreatic body and tail, similar to the prior study.  There is unchanged mild
dilatation of the main pancreatic duct.  Previously seen intraductal stones
are less well demonstrated on the present study.  Multiple cystic lesions in
the pancreatic tail are unchanged.

Spleen: There is moderate splenomegaly with the spleen measuring up to 16.8
cm.  Accessory spleen is incidentally noted.

Adrenal Glands: Unremarkable.

Kidneys: Simple renal cysts are present bilaterally.  There is no suspicious
lesion or hydronephrosis.

Gastrointestinal Tract:  The stomach, small bowel, and colon are grossly
unremarkable.

Lymph Nodes: No suspicious adenopathy.

Vasculature: Unremarkable.

Osseous and Soft Tissue Structures: No suspicious osseous lesion.  There are
mild-to-moderate degenerative changes of the lumbar spine.

1. Multiple subcentimeter new hepatic microabscesses in segment VIII.  No
drainable fluid collection.

findings of mild cholangitis, diffuse left hepatic atrophy with irregular mild
biliary ductal dilatation, splenomegaly, and sequelae of prior pancreatitis.

PTBD Placement

COMPARISON:  MRI of the abdomen dated ___

TECHNIQUE:   OPERATORS: Dr. ___ Interventional ___
and Dr. ___, Interventional Radiology fellow performed the
procedure. Dr. ___ supervised the trainee during any key
components of the procedure where applicable and reviewed and agrees with the
findings as reported below.
ANESTHESIA: General endotracheal anesthesia
MEDICATIONS: 2 g of ceftriaxone
CONTRAST: 40 ml of Optiray contrast
FLUOROSCOPY TIME AND DOSE:  52 minutes, 1142 mGy


PROCEDURE:
1. Transabdominal ultrasound.
2. Ultrasound and Fluoroscopic guided right percutaneous transhepatic bile
duct access.
3. Right cholangiogram
4. Right cholangio cone beam CT
5. ___ right biliary drain placement.

PROCEDURE DETAILS:
Following the discussion of the risks, benefits, and alternatives to the
procedure, written informed consent was obtained from the patient. The patient
was then brought to the angiography suite and placed supine on the exam table.
General endotracheal anesthesia was induced a pre-procedure time-out was
performed per ___ protocol. The right abdomen was prepped and draped in the
usual sterile fashion.
Under ultrasound Guidance a 21 gauge cook needle was advanced into the liver
to cannulate a candidate biliary duct however was unsuccessful.  This was
repeated twice and then a combined ultrasound fluoroscopic approach was
pursued.  Under Ultrasound and Fluoroscopic guidance, a 21G Cook needle was
advanced into the rightbiliary stent.  Images of the access were stored on
PACS.  Contrast was injected opacifying the biliary system.  A two stick
technique was used to access a more peripheral biliary duct more cranially
under fluoroscopic Guidance.  A 21 gauge cook needle was used to access the
more peripheral cranial duct.  A headliner Wire was advanced through the
needle centrally.  The metal stiffener and inner dilator of the Accustick were
advanced however were not successfully negotiated centrally and buckled into
adjacent branches.  The Accustick was removed and re-assembled in attempt to
negotiate the sheath centrally however was unsuccessful.  The inner dilator
and metal stiffener and Wire were removed.  This access was used to opacify
the biliary duct.  Rotational cone-beam CT angiography was performed to help
delineate the anatomy.  Multiplanar CT images were reconstructed and 3D
volume-rendered images of the biliary anatomy required post-processing on an
independent workstation under direct physician ___.  These images were
used in the interpretation, decision making for intervention and reporting of
this procedure. a third access was obtained more caudally at a more favorable
angle.  A headliner microwire was advanced into the duodenum after numerous
attempts.  An Accustick set was advanced over the head liner.  The metal
stiffener and inner dilator were removed.  A rotating hemostatic valve was
attached to the outer sheath with the indwelling headliner in place to secure
the access.  Contrast was injected confirming appropriate positioning.  The
microwire and hemostatic valve were removed.  A stiff Glidewire was advanced
through the Accustick outer sheath into the duodenum.  The sheath was advanced
into the duodenum.  The Wire was exchanged for an Amplatz Wire which was
coiled into the duodenum.  The sheath was then exchanged for a 10 ___ the
strong biliary drain.  The Wire and inner stiffener were removed.  Contrast
was injected confirming appropriate positioning.  The Catheter was secured to
the skin with an 0 silk suture and a StatLock.  The central access was
removed.  The peripheral access was embolized with Gel-Foam under fluoroscopic
Guidance.  Sterile dressing was applied.  The drain was attached to a Bag. The
patient tolerated the procedure well.  There were no immediate complications.

FINDINGS:


1. Fluoroscopic images demonstrate successful access of the central biliary
duct through the right hepatic biliary stent and successful opacification of
the biliary tree with passage of contrast into the duodenum.
2. Spot fluoroscopic images demonstrates successful access of a peripheral
cranial biliary duct along the right anterior biliary system.
3. Cone beam CT demonstrates successful access of right anterior biliary
ducts.  The opacified ducts are in similar segments 5 and 8 where biliary
micro abscesses were seen on recent MRI.  No evidence of bowel transgression
through the access.
4. Spot images demonstrate successful passage of a glidewire and Accustick
outer sheath into the duodenum.
5. Final spot fluoroscopic images demonstrate appropriate positioning of right
PTBD.
6. Fluoroscopic cine demonstrates Gel-Foam embolization of cranial peripheral
biliary duct access tract.

IMPRESSION: 

Successful placement of the right ___ F internal-external biliary drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, I'm Dr. Patel. You were admitted with fever and nausea. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling much better. The fever broke after they gave me Tylenol in the ER. But I was really shaky and tired this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your temperature was 101.6 in the ER, and your heart rate was high. We’ve restarted the same antibiotics you were on before—ceftazidime-avibactam and metronidazole—because of your history with resistant E. coli.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was done with IV antibiotics. I just finished a four-week course a few weeks ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know, and we hoped this wouldn’t come back. But given your history, we need to act quickly. We’re waiting on blood cultures, but we’re treating this as a recurrence of infection until proven otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t have any belly pain this time, which is different. Last time it was sharp and on the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s actually common. With your stents and chronic issues, infections don’t always present the same way. We’re going to get an MRI tomorrow to check your liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. Johnson. Your MRI results are back. There are several very small abscesses in your liver—microabscesses—mostly in the upper right lobe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Are they draining them? Like last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. These are too small to drain directly. But they’re a sign that your bile isn’t draining well, which is allowing bacteria to grow. We’re going to involve interventional radiology to place a biliary drain to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another drain? I had one before. Is this permanent?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an external drain for now. It will help decompress your bile ducts and reduce the risk of future infections. It’s not permanent, but it may stay in for several months depending on how things go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I have to take IV antibiotics the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We plan to continue IV antibiotics for four weeks. After that, we’ll repeat the MRI. If the abscesses are gone, we may stop them. But we’ll need to keep your bile flowing well to prevent recurrence.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And what about my other meds? I stopped apixaban and ursodiol after my last appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ah, that’s important. You should have stayed on both. Apixaban prevents clots in your portal vein, and ursodiol helps thin your bile. We’re restarting both today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought the doctor told me to stop them. I must have misunderstood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an easy mix-up. We’ll make sure your instructions are clear this time. We don’t want you at risk for another clot or bile sludge buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We reviewed your case with GI, interventional radiology, and liver surgery. They agree the best step is a percutaneous biliary drain on the right side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Scheduled for Thursday—February 5th. First, we’ll place a PICC line so you can get your antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another line in my arm? I had one before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in your left upper arm. It’s the safest way to give the antibiotics over four weeks. The team will place it on Wednesday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi Mr. Johnson. The PICC line was placed successfully this morning. The chest X-ray confirms it’s in the right spot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel a thing. Is it okay to move my arm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, gentle movement is fine. Just keep the dressing dry and let us know if it becomes red, swollen, or painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the drain procedure is tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll be under general anesthesia. The radiologist will place a tube through your liver into the bile duct to help drain the bile externally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt afterward?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You may have some soreness, but we’ll give you pain medication. Most patients tolerate it well. The goal is to prevent more infections like this one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re back. The procedure went well. You now have a right-sided biliary drain. It’s draining green bile, which is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel groggy, but okay. Is the tube going to be like this forever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not forever. It’s secured with a suture and a device called a StatLock. You’ll go home with it and learn how to care for it with a nurse’s help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics continue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, IV ceftazidime-avibactam every eight hours and oral metronidazole three times a day for four weeks. A nurse will deliver the IV meds to your home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my blood counts? My hemoglobin was low last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have iron deficiency anemia. We gave you an IV iron infusion yesterday. You’re scheduled for another one in the clinic next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been so tired lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be from the anemia or the infection. We’ll monitor your labs closely. Your platelets are also low, but stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your latest blood culture came back negative—no bacteria grew. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll make sure you’re comfortable managing the drain and getting your IV meds at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, in four weeks. We’ll check if the microabscesses have resolved. Then you’ll see Dr. Lee in clinic to decide if you can stop antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my cancer? Is it still stable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your last scans showed no evidence of disease. You’re on surveillance with alternating MRI and CT every six months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried it came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Understandable, but right now, this infection is separate. We’re focused on clearing it and preventing recurrence with the drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Johnson, you’re cleared to go home today. Your condition is stable, and you’re no longer febrile.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you develop fever, chills, belly pain, or if the drain stops draining or becomes red or tender. Keep the site clean and dry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A nurse will visit daily to give your IV antibiotic and check the line. Don’t get it wet. Report any swelling, redness, or pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be on insulin soon. My sugar’s been high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose was 166 on admission—elevated but not critical. Your primary doctor will manage that. Keep monitoring at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other pills—can I take them all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications are continued, including apixaban, ursodiol, and your prostate and allergy meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send a summary to your doctors. You’ll have follow-up in a week with the liver team and your next iron infusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot. We’re glad we could help. Take care, and call with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge instructions are written out. A nurse will go over them with you before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I want to make sure I understand everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. That’s our goal—safe recovery at home with full support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel confident now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’ll be here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—can I travel for my grandson’s birthday in six weeks?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s see how you’re doing after the MRI and clinic visit. If everything looks good, short travel may be possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll wait to book anything then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Smart plan. Focus on healing first.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team will arrive in an hour to take you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember, call us with any fever or issues with the drain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our pleasure. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be here.

summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a patient with metastatic cholangiocarcinoma on surveillance and a history of recurrent cholangitis due to multidrug-resistant E. coli, was admitted with fever and nausea. He had recently completed a four-week course of IV antibiotics for a hepatic abscess but had inadvertently stopped apixaban and ursodiol. On admission, he was restarted on ceftazidime-avibactam and metronidazole. MRI revealed new subcentimeter liver microabscesses. A multidisciplinary team decided to place a percutaneous transhepatic biliary drain to improve biliary drainage and prevent recurrence. A PICC line was placed for IV antibiotic administration. He was discharged home on a four-week course of IV and oral antibiotics, with plans for follow-up MRI and clinic visit. His portal vein thrombosis was managed with apixaban, and iron deficiency anemia was addressed with IV iron infusions.
